unit.title: Seva, the Golden Temple, and Gratitude

contentBlocks.text: Last week you practiced a simple, personal prayer. Today: a special kind of prayer Sikhs often say together, standing, called Ardas.

Ardas is a prayer Sikhs say together, usually standing, as a way of giving thanks and asking for guidance — often at the end of a Gurdwara service, or before starting something important. Saying Ardas together, standing, is itself meaningful: it shows everyone pausing together with a shared sense of gratitude and hope. Think of one moment in your own life — starting something new, or finishing something important — where pausing to feel grateful might feel meaningful.
You now understand Ardas as a real, shared practice of gratitude and guidance. Tomorrow we'll bring everything from this week together.

objectives: Describe Ardas as a shared, standing prayer of thanks and guidance
Connect the idea of pausing for gratitude to a real personal moment
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review last week's simple personal prayer moment.
2. Introduce Ardas as a shared, standing prayer of thanks and guidance.
3. Discuss when Ardas is typically said (end of a service, before something important).
4. Have the child identify a personal moment where pausing for gratitude would feel meaningful.
5. Complete the worksheet.
6. Preview tomorrow's synthesis lesson.
differentiationTips: Struggling: focus on the simple idea of 'pausing together to feel thankful' rather than the specific term Ardas
Ready for more: ask the child to compare Ardas (said together, standing) to last week's Simran-style personal prayer (quiet, individual)

This lesson is deliberately conceptual — it describes what Ardas is and when it's said, without reciting or paraphrasing any of its actual text, consistent with the no-fabrication discipline for religious content
teacherGuide.answerKey: This is a discussion and drawing activity — check that the child can describe Ardas as a shared, standing prayer of thanks and guidance, and identify a real personal moment for gratitude.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses the course's 'simple prayers' description, introducing a real, communal form of prayer alongside last week's individual, quiet practice — kept conceptual and experiential rather than reciting specific text.

rows.problem: Name one moment in your own life where pausing for gratitude would feel meaningful.
